report.source_text: On the evening of admission, the patient developed an acute feeling of illness, worsening nausea and vomiting, vertigo, perioral and left-hand numbness, and light-headedness. The primary team called the neurology team, stating that she had worsening mental status and had become more somnolent. She was then transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU) for neuro checks every hour. A CT angiogram was ordered and showed stable findings compared to the morning. Her neurologic exam at this time was significant for disorientation where she was confused as to where she was, bradyphrenia, moderate-severe dysarthria with trouble remembering words and muffled speech, left-sided ptosis, and bilateral mild ataxia with finger-nose-finger.

report.source_text: Our neurology team was in contact with the interventional radiology team, and, after a discussion with the patient and her family, it was decided that interventional radiology would perform a mechanical thrombectomy. The procedure was started within an hour of these new symptoms onset. The patient tolerated the procedure with no acute complications and was sent back to the ICU for monitoring. The heparin drip was restarted immediately after the procedure.

clinician.trajectory_summary: An 83-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation and recent cessation of rivaroxaban presented with nausea, left-sided tingling, dry mouth, and mild dysarthria. Initial NIHSS was 1, with no motor weakness and GCS 15. CT angiogram on admission revealed occlusion of the distal basilar artery and a perfusion deficit in the right superior cerebellar artery. Later on admission, neurological symptoms worsened with disorientation, bradyphrenia, moderate-severe dysarthria, left ptosis, and mild ataxia, prompting ICU transfer. Mechanical thrombectomy was performed promptly after symptom worsening, tolerated well, and anticoagulation was restarted. The patient's visual hallucinations and dizziness resolved shortly after and she was discharged after stabilization. Six weeks post-discharge follow-up revealed complete neurological recovery with no residual deficits.
